title: Favoritism
english: The brothers of Joseph hated him and were unable to speak to him in a peaceful manner.

The writer of the book of Genesis has made an exact enumeration of those who came from Esau, including their descendants and the places where they settled, as well as the rule they received, which the scripture has taught us.
However, the scripture does not record any notable or memorable deeds of these people.
Instead, it focuses on the story of Joseph, who was the youngest of his brothers and yet showed remarkable maturity and wisdom beyond his years.
Joseph was seventeen years old and was already involved in pastoral work, taking care of his father's flocks, and he was not idle, but rather worked hard and was responsible.
His father, Jacob, loved him dearly and saw in him a son of his old age, as it says, 'a son of his old age' (Genesis 37:3).
The word of God is concerned with the dispositions in us, and how we respond to those who are younger or older than us.
Human nature has a tendency to overpower and coerce the mind, often leading to a slight concession to the weaker ones, as they are in need of frugality.
This can be seen in the way that affection is distributed among children, with the excess of love being reserved for the last one.

The human mind is fond of novelty, and this is evident in the way that it does not reject the abundance of those who have already gone, but is greatly changed by those who are not yet present or have just been acquired.
This phenomenon can be observed in the story of Jacob, who loved Joseph more than his other sons because he was his old age son.
Despite having previously married Leah in Haran, Jacob's love for Rachel, who bore Joseph, was evident, and he was deeply affected by her death in childbirth, when she gave birth to Benjamin.
Joseph's natural disposition was not equal to everyone, and the old man showed it to be diverse, as if it had been inclined towards him.

As Joseph grew into a mature man, his character and abilities became increasingly evident, and it is likely that he would become a great and famous person, probably reasoning that he would be illustrious and famous.
translator_notes: The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off at the end.
The translation of some words, such as 'εἰρηνικόν', may have multiple possible renderings, but 'peaceful' seems to be the most appropriate in this context.
The allusion to Genesis 37:4 is based on the similarity in language and context, but it is not a direct quote.
The reference to Genesis 36 is based on the content of the chapter, which lists the descendants of Esau.
The translation of ἄμφω μὲν ἤστην γήρως υἱώ is uncertain, but it appears to refer to both Joseph and Benjamin being old age sons.
The text seems to be missing some words at the end of the last sentence, and the translation is therefore incomplete.

title: Christ's Glory
english: Christ's glory is multifaceted and is being marveled at in many ways because he is the source of life and also the light that illuminates those in darkness, much like he cleanses lepers and raises the dead with ease, even those who have begun to decay.

He is the one who rebukes the seas and is obeyed by the waves themselves, which is why the Jews, having been utterly perplexed and consumed by the fire of envy, were saying to each other, 'What are we doing? For this man is performing many signs.'

The multicolored tunic represents the many-formed glory that God and the Father has clothed the Son with, who became human for our sake, and since he himself is the Lord of glory, he can say, 'Father, glorify your Son,' reflecting his likeness to us.

Those who were once servants were being led into sorrows, and they had become suspicious due to the narration of dreams, foreseeing that they would be underfoot and objects of worship, while Christ would far surpass them and become an object of worship even to those who had given birth to him.

The Jews were being provoked and grieved, learning that the Emmanuel would surpass even the holy Fathers and would be an object of worship to all people, rather to the whole earth, as the blessed David openly declares that all the nations which God made will come and worship before Him, Lord (Psalm 86:9).

Understanding this, they were saying, 'This is the heir, come let us kill him and seize his inheritance,' demonstrating their envy and lawless anger against Christ, which is also revealed by David when he says, 'The Lord has reigned, let the peoples be angry' (Psalm 99:1).

Having shown the envy of the Jews, we must speak of their most hated and bloodthirsty attempts at the right time, pushing the narrative of history everywhere, and setting the goal of the incarnation of the Only-Begotten.

For the narrative leads us back to this: Joseph is sent to Shechem by his father's command to see how his brothers are and where they are pasturing, but he finds them in Dothan, and as they see him approaching, they mock him with bitter and hateful scorn, saying, 'Behold, that dreamer.'
